title: Impacts of diffuse pressure complexes complicate conservation and management of benthic marine habitats
content:
Our results suggest that pressures in marine ecosystems often arise from numerous seemingly minor activities that collectively contribute to substantial habitat degradation. They underscore the urgent need to develop more targeted, local management measures that address detrimental small-scale activities. In our study area, such measures could include regulating dredging (e.g. through permitting), limiting recreational boating in ecologically most sensitive areas, and developing guidelines for coastal development. Stricter regulation should be imposed particularly in areas with limited water exchange, where these activities likely amplify pressures on already degraded ecosystems.


Abstract

Human activities exert considerable pressures on marine ecosystems, causing widespread habitat loss (direct footprint) and degradation (diffuse pressures). Cumulative effect assessments are widely used to evaluate pressures, but their utility in spatial management remains limited due to their typically coarse resolution. Importantly, effects interpreted as additive or synergistic at broad scales may not be such when analysed with high-resolution data. We compiled high-resolution spatial data on human activities, capturing both coastal land use and activities at sea, and estimated their associated pressures and impacts on benthic ecosystems in Finland, northern Baltic Sea. Through hierarchical clustering, we identified ‘pressure complexes’, broader areas where different human activities co-occur with varying composition. We further evaluated eutrophication profiles of these clusters, the main environmental problem of the Baltic Sea, and quantified the relative severity of human activities on benthic habitats using detailed species distribution models. We identified three pressure clusters, primarily driven by recreational activities, industrial sea use, and maritime traffic. Many activities were spatially confined, especially in archipelago areas, but their diffuse pressures co-occurred, impacting the same region and similar habitats. Diffuse pressures had one to two orders of magnitude larger spatial impact on benthic habitats than activities causing direct habitat loss. Recreational activities and coastal land use emerged as the most detrimental drivers of habitat degradation, despite their limited spatial extent. Nutrient concentrations were elevated in all pressure clusters, indicating that diffuse pressures, caused by various human activities, act in synergy with coastal eutrophication, amplifying their effects and complicating their management. Policy implications. Our results suggest that pressures in marine ecosystems often arise from numerous seemingly minor activities that collectively contribute to substantial habitat degradation. They underscore the urgent need to develop more targeted, local management measures that address detrimental small-scale activities. In our study area, such measures could include regulating dredging (e.g. through permitting), limiting recreational boating in ecologically most sensitive areas, and developing guidelines for coastal development. Stricter regulation should be imposed particularly in areas with limited water exchange, where these activities likely amplify pressures on already degraded ecosystems.
